Sirius.headline: The brightest star in the night sky.
Sirius.color_reason: Blue-white because its surface is very hot, around 9,900 C.
Sirius.size_or_scale: About twice as massive as the Sun and roughly 25 times brighter.
Sirius.lore: In Indian sky tradition Sirius is Lubdhaka, the hunter following Mriga, the deer (Orion), across the night.
Sirius.binocular_tip: Brilliant white in binoculars; its white dwarf companion Sirius B is real but far too faint to see.

Canopus.headline: The second-brightest star in the night sky, and the brightest you never see from far northern latitudes.
Canopus.color_reason: Yellow-white, the colour of a bright supergiant.
Canopus.size_or_scale: Roughly 65 times wider than the Sun and thousands of times brighter.
Canopus.lore: Indian tradition names Canopus after Agastya, the revered sage who crossed the Vindhya mountains to the south.
Canopus.binocular_tip: Sits low in the south from India in winter; a clean horizon view is the prize.

Rigil Kentaurus.headline: The nearest star system to the Sun, just over 4 light years away.
Rigil Kentaurus.color_reason: Warm yellow-white like a Sun-like star slightly hotter than ours.
Rigil Kentaurus.size_or_scale: A triple system; its faint red member Proxima hosts the closest known exoplanet.
Rigil Kentaurus.binocular_tip: Visible only from the southern tropics and south; splits into two bright components in a small telescope.

Arcturus.headline: The brightest star of the northern spring and a nearby red giant.
Arcturus.color_reason: Orange because it is a cool giant, cooler than the Sun.
Arcturus.size_or_scale: About 25 times wider than the Sun; its light opened the 1933 Chicago World's Fair, beamed from a telescope 40 years after the 1893 fair.
Arcturus.lore: The nakshatra Swati is named after this orange beacon.
Arcturus.binocular_tip: Its colour is the whole show: a warm amber point against the spring sky.

Vega.headline: The brightest star of the northern summer and a former pole star.
Vega.color_reason: Blue-white because it is a hot young star.
Vega.size_or_scale: About 2.5 times wider than the Sun; it spins so fast it is visibly flattened.
Vega.lore: The nakshatra Abhijit honours Vega; around 12,000 BCE it was the pole star, and it will be again.
Vega.binocular_tip: Halfway between Vega and Altair the Milky Way's Great Rift shows its dark dust lanes.

Capella.headline: The 'Goat Star', actually a pair of giant binaries circling each other.
Capella.color_reason: Warm yellow like an aged Sun, seen from about 43 light years away.
Capella.size_or_scale: The two bright components together shine about 80 times brighter than the Sun.
Capella.binocular_tip: Low in the northeast on autumn evenings it flashes red and blue; that is our atmosphere, not the star.

Rigel.headline: The blue-white supergiant at Orion's foot, one of the most powerful stars you can see.
Rigel.color_reason: Blue-white because it is far hotter than the Sun.
Rigel.size_or_scale: Tens of thousands of times brighter than the Sun, from about 850 light years away.
Rigel.binocular_tip: Contrast its icy blue with orange Betelgeuse at Orion's opposite corner.

Procyon.headline: The Little Dog Star that rises before Sirius, its namesake.
Procyon.color_reason: Yellow-white, a hot star slightly hotter than the Sun.
Procyon.size_or_scale: Only 11.5 light years away, with its own white dwarf companion.
Procyon.binocular_tip: Forms the Winter Triangle with Sirius and Betelgeuse.

Betelgeuse.headline: The red supergiant at Orion's shoulder, a star near the end of its life.
Betelgeuse.color_reason: Orange-red because it is a cool supergiant, only about half as hot as the Sun.
Betelgeuse.size_or_scale: If it replaced the Sun, its surface would stretch past the orbit of Mars.
Betelgeuse.binocular_tip: Watch it over months; it is a slow, unpredictable variable star.

Achernar.headline: The end of the River Eridanus, the flattest bright star known.
Achernar.color_reason: Blue-white because it is very hot.
Achernar.size_or_scale: It spins so fast that its poles are far closer to its core than its equator.
Achernar.binocular_tip: Best from south of about 33 degrees north latitude.

Altair.headline: The eye of the Eagle, a fast-spinning nearby star.
Altair.color_reason: White with a hint of blue from its high surface temperature.
Altair.size_or_scale: Completes one spin in about 9 hours; its equator bulges visibly.
Altair.lore: The nakshatra Shravana, 'the listener', belongs to this star of the Eagle.
Altair.binocular_tip: Flanked by two fainter stars in a line, a handy pattern for confirming you found it.

Aldebaran.headline: The orange eye of the Bull, glaring at Orion like the star's name means.
Aldebaran.color_reason: Orange because it is a cool giant star.
Aldebaran.size_or_scale: About 45 times wider than the Sun, sitting 65 light years away.
Aldebaran.lore: The nakshatra Rohini, favourite of the Moon in Vedic stories, is this orange star.
Aldebaran.binocular_tip: Look beside it for the V-shaped Hyades cluster it merely lines up with.

Antares.headline: The red supergiant heart of Scorpius, whose name means 'rival of Mars'.
Antares.color_reason: Fiery red-orange because it is a cool supergiant.
Antares.size_or_scale: If it replaced the Sun, its surface would reach past the orbit of Mars.
Antares.lore: The nakshatra Jyeshtha, 'the eldest', crowns Scorpius with this red giant.
Antares.binocular_tip: When Mars passes nearby, compare their colours; the name Antares means exactly that contest.

Spica.headline: The wheat ear of the Maiden, a tight pair of hot blue stars.
Spica.color_reason: Blue-white because its surface is among the hottest of bright stars.
Spica.size_or_scale: Its two components orbit each other every four days.
Spica.lore: The nakshatra Chitra, 'the brilliant one', is this sparkling jewel of Virgo.
Spica.binocular_tip: Follow the Big Dipper's handle in a great arc to Arcturus, then speed on to Spica.

Pollux.headline: The brighter of the Gemini twins, an orange giant with a known planet.
Pollux.color_reason: Warm orange because it is a cool giant.
Pollux.size_or_scale: About 9 times wider than the Sun, 34 light years away.
Pollux.lore: The nakshatra Punarvasu, 'return of the light', is marked by the Gemini twins.
Pollux.binocular_tip: Compare its colour with icy Castor beside it.

Fomalhaut.headline: The lonely autumn star of the south, ringed by a great disk of dust.
Fomalhaut.color_reason: White with a touch of blue, a hot young star.
Fomalhaut.size_or_scale: A debris disk orbits it where planets are forming, like a young solar system.
Fomalhaut.binocular_tip: Nothing bright is nearby, which is why old skywatchers called it the Lonely One.

Deneb.headline: The tail of the Swan, one of the most luminous stars visible to the eye.
Deneb.color_reason: White-blue from its ferociously hot surface.
Deneb.size_or_scale: Shines with the light of roughly a hundred thousand Suns from about 2,600 light years away.
Deneb.binocular_tip: Sweep around it: the Milky Way runs right through Cygnus.

Regulus.headline: The little king at the heart of Leo, sitting almost exactly on the Sun's yearly path.
Regulus.color_reason: Blue-white because it is hot and young.
Regulus.size_or_scale: It spins so fast it would fly apart if it spun much faster.
Regulus.lore: The nakshatra Magha, 'the royal one', is ruled by Regulus.
Regulus.binocular_tip: The Moon and planets pass right beside it, since it sits on the ecliptic.

Polaris.headline: The North Star, the anchor of every northern sky map.
Polaris.color_reason: Yellow-white, a supergiant far more luminous than it looks.
Polaris.size_or_scale: It stands almost exactly at the north celestial pole, less than a degree off.
Polaris.lore: Dhruva, the unmovable one, was the child devotee set in the sky forever by Vishnu.
Polaris.binocular_tip: Find it first: its height above the horizon equals your latitude.

Castor.headline: The twin's head that is actually a six-star family.
Castor.color_reason: White, hot and young like its brother Pollux's neighbour should be.
Castor.size_or_scale: Three pairs of stars bound together, all about 50 light years away.
Castor.binocular_tip: A small telescope splits its brightest pair.

Mizar.headline: The middle star of the Dipper's handle and history's most famous double star.
Mizar.color_reason: White-hot like a young A-type star.
Mizar.size_or_scale: Mizar itself is two stars, and its faint companion makes a famous pair.
Mizar.lore: Vasishtha is one of the seven sages riding the Saptarishi across the sky.
Mizar.binocular_tip: Look just beside it for faint Alcor; seeing both was a traditional eyesight test.

Alcor.headline: The faint little companion of Mizar, famous as an ancient vision test.
Alcor.color_reason: A white star much fainter than its bright partner.
Alcor.size_or_scale: Only about 4th magnitude, yet easy beside brilliant Mizar.
Alcor.lore: Arundhati, wife of sage Vasishtha, rides beside him; couples are still shown this pair at weddings as a model of companionship.
Alcor.binocular_tip: Any binoculars separate it instantly; bare eyes see it as one star if your sight is average.

Alcyone.headline: The brightest member of the Pleiades.
Alcyone.color_reason: Blue-white, a hot young star barely 100 million years old.
Alcyone.size_or_scale: About ten times wider than the Sun and a thousand times brighter.
Alcyone.binocular_tip: Binoculars reveal dozens more sisters around it.

Bellatrix.headline: The blue 'Amazon Star' at Orion's other shoulder.
Bellatrix.color_reason: Blue-white because it is a hot giant.
Bellatrix.size_or_scale: About 8 times wider than the Sun but far hotter and brighter.
Bellatrix.binocular_tip: Compare with orange Betelgeuse diagonally opposite; same constellation, opposite colours.

Adhara.headline: The second-brightest of Canis Major and the sky's brightest ultraviolet beacon.
Adhara.color_reason: Blue-white, one of the hottest bright stars.
Adhara.size_or_scale: A supergiant about 430 light years away, far beyond Sirius.
Adhara.binocular_tip: Forms a tidy triangle with Sirius and Wezen on winter evenings.

Andromeda Galaxy.headline: The farthest thing most human eyes can see: a whole galaxy 2.5 million light years away.
Andromeda Galaxy.size_or_scale: About a trillion stars; it and the Milky Way will merge in roughly 4.5 billion years.
Andromeda Galaxy.binocular_tip: Find the Great Square of Pegasus, hop to its upper-left star and glide two more fists in the same direction.

Great Orion Nebula.headline: A stellar nursery hanging from Orion's belt, visible to the naked eye as a fuzzy 'sword' star.
Great Orion Nebula.size_or_scale: About 1,350 light years away, where hundreds of new stars are forming right now.
Great Orion Nebula.binocular_tip: Look below Orion's Belt for three fainter stars in a line; the middle one is not a star.

Pleiades.headline: The Seven Sisters, a dipper-shaped cluster of young blue stars.
Pleiades.size_or_scale: About 440 light years away and roughly 100 million years old.
Pleiades.lore: Krittika, the nakshatra of fire, belongs to the Pleiades; legend says the six sisters were so shy that one hid away.
Pleiades.binocular_tip: Binoculars turn 6 stars into dozens wrapped in faint blue haze.

Ring Nebula.headline: A dying sun-like star that puffed off a perfect smoke ring of gas.
Ring Nebula.size_or_scale: About 2,300 light years away; this is our Sun's own distant future.
Ring Nebula.binocular_tip: Between the bottom two stars of Lyra's parallelogram; small but unmistakable in a telescope.

Crab Nebula.headline: The wreckage of a star that Chinese and Japanese astronomers saw explode in 1054 CE.
Crab Nebula.size_or_scale: A spinning pulsar at its core flashes 30 times every second.
Crab Nebula.binocular_tip: Near the star marking the Bull's northern horn; needs a dark, clear night even for a faint smudge.

Great Hercules Cluster.headline: A ball of several hundred thousand ancient stars, one of the sky's grandest sights.
Great Hercules Cluster.size_or_scale: About 22,000 light years away, older than the Sun by billions of years.
Great Hercules Cluster.binocular_tip: Between the stars of the Keystone in Hercules; half-moon shaped in binoculars, glorious in a telescope.

Lagoon Nebula.headline: A glowing cloud of gas where new stars are born, in the Teapot's steam.
Lagoon Nebula.size_or_scale: About 4,000 light years away, big enough to hold several Orion Nebulas.
Lagoon Nebula.binocular_tip: Just above the Teapot's top; binoculars show a bright patch with a dark lane through it.

Dumbbell Nebula.headline: The first planetary nebula ever discovered, a dying star's expanding cocoon.
Dumbbell Nebula.size_or_scale: About 1,350 light years away in the constellation Vulpecula, the little Fox.
Dumbbell Nebula.binocular_tip: Between Cygnus and Sagitta; binoculars catch it as a faint apple-shaped glow.

Whirlpool Galaxy.headline: The first galaxy ever recognized as a spiral, in 1845.
Whirlpool Galaxy.size_or_scale: About 23 million light years away, tugged by a small companion galaxy.
Whirlpool Galaxy.binocular_tip: Near the end star of the Big Dipper's handle; a telescope on a dark night shows the spiral.

Sombrero Galaxy.headline: A galaxy seen edge-on, wearing a brim of dark dust.
Sombrero Galaxy.size_or_scale: About 30 million light years away, with a central bulge hosting a massive black hole.
Sombrero Galaxy.binocular_tip: Just south of the Spica-to-Arcturus line; best with a telescope on a dark night.

Mercury.headline: The smallest planet and the fastest, hugging the Sun so tightly it is rarely seen.
Mercury.size_or_scale: Swings from -170 C at night to 430 C by day, the wildest temperature range of any planet.
Mercury.lore: Budha, the quick-witted son of Chandra, lends his name to Wednesday, Budhavar.
Mercury.binocular_tip: Catch it only in twilight, low near the horizon, for a couple of weeks at a time.

Venus.headline: The brightest planet, the 'evening star' or 'morning star'.
Venus.size_or_scale: Its runaway greenhouse keeps the surface near 465 C, hot enough to melt lead.
Venus.lore: Shukra, the guru of the demons, gives Venus its name and Friday, Shukravar, its day.
Venus.binocular_tip: A small telescope shows phases like a tiny Moon; check it a month apart.

Mars.headline: The red planet, glowing like a steady ember in the night.
Mars.size_or_scale: Rusty iron oxide dust paints it red; it is the second smallest planet.
Mars.lore: Mangal, the fierce one, lends Mars its name and Tuesday, Mangalavar, its day.
Mars.binocular_tip: Its brightness changes hugely from year to year as the two planets' orbits line up.

Jupiter.headline: The king of planets, bright enough to outshine every star in the sky.
Jupiter.size_or_scale: More than 1,300 Earths would fit inside; its Great Red Spot is a storm wider than Earth.
Jupiter.lore: Brihaspati, guru of the gods, gives Jupiter its name and Thursday, Guruvar, its day.
Jupiter.binocular_tip: Any binoculars held steady show its four Galilean moons as a little line of stars; watch them swap sides over days.

Saturn.headline: The ringed jewel of the solar system.
Saturn.size_or_scale: Its rings are ice and rock spanning 280,000 km, yet mostly just tens of metres thick.
Saturn.lore: Shani, the slow judge of deeds, gives Saturn its name and Saturday, Shanivar, its day.
Saturn.binocular_tip: Hold binoculars very steady and the rings make it look like a tiny oval; a small telescope makes them unmistakable.

Moon.headline: Earth's companion, close enough to see craters with the naked eye.
Moon.size_or_scale: About 384,000 km away, so its light reaches you in about 1.3 seconds.
Moon.lore: Chandra rides a chariot of white horses across the night; many nakshatras are his brides in myth.
Moon.binocular_tip: Along the terminator, the line between light and dark, shadows make craters leap out in 3-D.

Orion.headline: The hunter, the easiest constellation to recognize anywhere in the sky.
Orion.size_or_scale: It holds two of the sky's ten brightest stars and the great Orion Nebula.
Orion.lore: Mriga, the deer, is chased forever across the sky by Lubdhaka, the hunter dog that is Sirius.
Orion.binocular_tip: Sweep below the Belt for the Orion Nebula; nothing else in the sky looks like it.

Ursa Major.headline: The Great Bear, home of the Big Dipper or Saptarishi.
Ursa Major.size_or_scale: From India it never sets; the whole pattern wheels around Polaris all night.
Ursa Major.lore: Seven sages, the Saptarishi, ride this pattern around the pole: Marichi, Vasishtha, Angiras, Atri, Pulastya, Pulaha and Kratu.
Ursa Major.binocular_tip: Mizar in the handle shows a faint companion, Arundhati, beside it.

Crux.headline: The Southern Cross, the smallest constellation in the sky and the most famous.
Crux.size_or_scale: It appears on five national flags, from Australia and New Zealand to Brazil.
Crux.binocular_tip: Its long axis points toward the south celestial pole, where there is no pole star.

Scorpius.headline: The scorpion with a red heart and a hooked tail.
Scorpius.size_or_scale: It lies close to the brightest part of the Milky Way's centre.
Scorpius.binocular_tip: Follow the curved tail low in the south on summer nights; each curl holds a star cluster.

Sagittarius.headline: The archer whose Teapot points the way to the centre of our galaxy.
Sagittarius.size_or_scale: The Milky Way is densest here because you are looking toward the galactic core.
Sagittarius.binocular_tip: Sweep the 'steam' rising from the Teapot's spout for nebulae and clusters.

Big Dipper.headline: Seven bright stars that point the way north.
Big Dipper.size_or_scale: The two outer bowl stars, Merak and Dubhe, point to Polaris five fists away.
Big Dipper.lore: The seven sages in their sky chariot, circling Dhruva, the pole star.
Big Dipper.binocular_tip: Look at the middle of the handle for Mizar and Alcor, the famous eye test pair.

Orion's Belt.headline: Three stars in a straight line, the most useful signpost in the sky.
Orion's Belt.size_or_scale: The three stars are hundreds of light years away and unrelated, yet line up perfectly from here.
Orion's Belt.binocular_tip: Below the Belt hangs the sword with the Orion Nebula in its middle.

Summer Triangle.headline: Three bright stars from three constellations ruling summer evenings.
Summer Triangle.size_or_scale: Vega, Deneb and Altair are 25, 2,600 and 17 light years away, yet look equally bright.
Summer Triangle.binocular_tip: The Milky Way flows through the Triangle, splitting near Altair into two dark channels.

Southern Cross.headline: The smallest constellation, and the southern sky's compass.
Southern Cross.size_or_scale: Its long axis points within a few degrees of the south celestial pole.
Southern Cross.binocular_tip: The jewel box cluster sparkles just beside its eastern arm in binoculars.
